new_statements.quote: Stress is indicated with the acute accent (´); e.g., -póaka 'scream,' -poáka 'already poured out.' However, stress may optionally be left unmarked in the following "regular" cases: where the penultimate vowel is different from the final vowel, stress is generally on the penultimate syllable (e.g. -leha (-léha) 'ask,' bole (bóle) 'banana'); and where the penultimate vowel is the same as the final vowel, stress is on the antepenultimate syllable (e.g., -poaka (-póaka) 'scream,' baluhu (báluhu) 'adult') unless there are only two syllables, in which case it is on the penultimate (e.g., peke (péke)).
new_statements.citation: Taylor, Paul Michael. 1990. The Folk Biology of the Tobelo People: A Study in Folk Classification. (Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 34.) Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution Press.

It agrees with the penultimate main rule in Hueting 1908 (Inleiding p. 6, downloaded in the 2026-09-16 independent check recorded in : 'Als hoofdregel voor den klemtoon kan gelden, dat deze valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep.. Wanneer bij woorden, bestaande uit drie of meer lettergrepen, de laatste lettergreep een stommen vocaal heeft, telt die lettergreep niet mee voor den klemtoon') and states the antepenult subcase in phonemic terms (final vowel identical to the penultimate vowel) rather than Hueting's 'mute vowel' final; both descriptions skip a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress. In words of three or more syllables whose final vowel copies the penultimate vowel (an echo-vowel final, e.g. baluhu, -poaka, ngunungu), stress moves one syllable left to the antepenult, i.e. the echo-vowel final syllable is skipped; disyllables are always penultimate (péke). Placement is thus predictable from the segmental shape in the 'regular' cases, and Taylor marks the acute only where a word departs from them.
new_statements.exceptions: Yes: 'generally' and 'regular cases' imply lexical exceptions, which Taylor marks with the acute; his own example -poáka 'already poured out' (final vowel = penult vowel, so the rule predicts antepenult -póaka as in 'scream') is such an exception, i.e. a minimal pair -póaka 'scream' vs -poáka 'already poured out'. Elsewhere (p. 40, 'Influences on Tobelo nomenclature') he notes that the final unstressed/unaccented echo syllable is dropped in Ternatese-style compounds (ngunungu 'nose' > ngunu-, glama > gla), consistent with that syllable being outside the stress domain.
new_statements.identity_note: Taylor 1990 writes Tobelo 'in a phonemic transcription.. reflecting Boeng dialect pronunciation' (p. vii) and states that his terminology is valid for the Dodinga dialect (Pasir Putih, Dodinga District) unless noted otherwise, with earlier fieldwork in Boeng-dialect villages (p. 4, sec. 1.x); he contrasts these with Hueting's (1908) Tobelo District (H) dialect and notes only minor phonological differences between dialects (h ~ f ~ s). The stress statement is not restricted to one dialect.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the PDF we hold/scanned/page scan of Hueting 1936 at BKI 94 pp. 324-325 (PDF 378-379), and the p.297 supporting remark is also there; the record's paraphrase of rules I-V and the two-domain suffix statement is faithful. (2) The classification rests on a 1936 Dutch missionary grammar sketch with an explicit stress chapter — first-hand and specific, so nothing suggests it is wrong, but it is 90 years old, impressionistic, and its weight clause is the author's historical rationalisation of diphthongs as contracted V+V. The one modern grammar (Holton 2003, Lincom, 99 pp) is not yet obtained and not open; no phonology article or instrumental study of Tobelo appears in Glottolog 5.1 (28 entries scanned) or on the WALS page, and WALS/StressTyp2 themselves rest on Hueting 1908/1936.
